title: the sweet smoke of Putana's pyre
hookLine: Putana's pyre smells sweet, and the narrator says even she reached a mother's place
carry: his grace answers even a poisoned offering

cards: The cowherd women snatch the baby off Putana's body and carry him away, shaking. Then they protect him the way they know how.

The Bhagavata describes it closely: they wave a cow's tail around him, wash him, mark his body with the dust of cows, and touch his limbs one by one while saying names of Vishnu, asking each name to guard a part of him.
Heart. Then Yashoda nurses him to sleep. The danger is over.

teach.b: Nanda comes home from Mathura with the other cowherds and finds a giant body lying across the village. He remembers Vasudeva's warning and is amazed: the man saw it coming.
The cowherds cut up the body, pile it on a fire and burn it.
And the smoke smells sweet, rising fragrant, the Bhagavata says, like aloe wood. Why would a child-killer's pyre smell like incense?
The text gives its own answer: because the child had drunk her milk, her wrongs were burned away. Then the narrator, the sage Shuka, says something astonishing. Putana came to kill.
She smeared poison on her breast and offered it to the Lord.

teach.h: SHUKA: SHE REACHED A MOTHER'S PLACE
teach.b: Even so, because she offered him milk, she reached the place given to a mother. If even she, who came with murder in mind, was given that, Shuka asks, what of those who offer him love? That is the hinge.
The Bhagavata doesn't dwell on punishing her. It dwells on the one thing she did that looked like a mother's act, and treats it as hers.
Hindus call this kripa, the Lord's grace, and some Vaishnava teachers read Putana as its clearest picture: he answers the offering itself, and his touch transforms even an offering made in bad faith.
So the same story holds both: the village's right to guard what it loves with every name it knows, and a mercy wider than anyone there expected.

how: Vaishnava teachers and devotees retell Putana's story as an example of Krishna's grace, and the protective rites the cowherd women perform are described in the Bhagavata alongside the names of Vishnu they recite.

games.q: you're one of the cowherd women. the baby is safe, lying on the body of the woman who tried to kill him. what do you do first?
o: pick him up and guard him with Vishnu's names.
run to Mathura to tell Nanda.
games.why: they take him up and perform protective rites, touching each limb with a name of Vishnu, and Yashoda nurses him to sleep.

practice: First, like the cowherd women, bring to mind someone you want to protect, and hold them for a few breaths.
Then, more slowly, bring to mind someone you find difficult; no need to like them or excuse anything, just notice one thing they ever did that was not cruel, and let that small thing be true too.
If you pray, you can hold both people in your prayer.
